messages:
emma: Quick question — trying to capture a short nsys trace that shows when KV cache eviction kicks in during a burst. I want nvtx + osrt + cuda but keep the QDREP tiny. Current cmd: `nsys profile -o evict.qdrep --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt --sample=none --duration=5s` — but I'm missing the kernel handoff (it happens a bit later). Any tips?

raj: bracket the region with NVTX markers instead of relying on wall-clock duration. push/pop around the batch that causes eviction and use `--capture-range=nvtx`. That way you capture precisely what matters and file sizes stay small. :thumbsup:

mike: example pattern we use: instrument the code where you detect a cache miss spike and add an NVTX range there. e.g. in python with cupy/pynvtx:```python
import nvtx
nvtx.range_push("KV_EVICT_BRACKET")
# run the risky batch
nvtx.range_pop()
```
Then run: `nsys profile -o evict.qdrep --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt --capture-range=nvtx --sample=none`

sasha: if the eviction is non-deterministic (timing jitter) do a two-step: warmup + bracket. warmup to get the system into the same state (kernels loaded, caches hot) then open the NVTX bracket. Short-duration bracketed captures are much more repeatable.

emma: useful — in our runs the eviction happens ~1.5s after the first big batch, so a 5s overall duration misses it. If I NVTX-wrap the offending batch it should catch it even if jitter shifts it a bit, right?

raj: yep. also consider sampling vs continuous collection: `--sample=none` = full timestamps for osrt which is great but produces bigger files. If you only need a flamegraph-ish hotspot view use `--sample=cpu` or `--sample=clock` and a lower frequency. For kernel handoff timing you usually want continuous for the short bracket.

mike: another trick: emit a lightweight NVTX event right before and after the KV cache eviction codepath (not just the batch). that gives you exact markers in the timeline and you can quickly zoom to the tiny window in the Nsight UI.

emma: any advice on osrt markers? I remember some of our kernels show up as generic "unknown" without the OSRT annotations.

sasha: ensure the runtime is built with OSRT hooks enabled and that `--trace=osrt` is present. Also add NVTX annotations around high-level ops so the OSRT lanes map to meaningful ranges. If a kernel still shows as unknown, check that symbolization was done (container has debug symbols or `cuobjdump`-based symbolization enabled).

perf-bot: quick checklist: 1) bracket with NVTX, 2) warmup run before capture, 3) use `--trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt`, 4) if file size too big, switch to sampling for the non-bracket runs, 5) filter kernels >1ms in UI.

emma: helpful — thanks. One more: when I do bracketed capture I sometimes still see a bunch of tiny kernel noise that hides the eviction kernel in timeline. Any filtering tips?

raj: in the Nsight timeline use the Kernel events filter and set min duration to something like 200us or 1ms depending on your workload. Also group kernels by name and sort by total time — eviction-related kernels often pop to the top. If you need to programmatically trim qdrep, you can export the timeline to CSV and filter offline.

mike: if the eviction involves a big memcpy or a fallback kernel, look for correlation ids crossing streams — use the stream lanes view and enable "show correlations". That usually reveals the handoff between the batch-serving kernel and the eviction/evict-cleanup kernel.

emma: great pointers. I'll instrument NVTX around the suspect code, do a warmup, run with `--capture-range=nvtx --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt --sample=none` and filter kernels >200us. I'll report back with qdrep size and screenshots. Thanks y'all :rocket:

nsys-bot: capture completed: evict.qdrep saved (estimated 96MB) — use Nsight Systems to open and inspect timeline.
